newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to issue report on EMU accounting rules.
newsitem.headline: EU to issue report on EMU accounting rules.

text.p: Eurostat, the European Union's statistical office, will offer an assessment next week of the accounting practices EU governments have used to meet the preconditions of a single currency.

EU officials said on Wednesday that the group will issue a report on Monday that clarifies whether certain practices are legitimate and can therefore be used by governments in bringing their deficits in line with the Maastricht treaty.
"There is a meeting of the Committee of Monetary, Financial and Balance of Payments Statistics on Thursday and Friday," said a spokeswoman for Eurostat.
She stressed, however, that the meeting was "consultative" and not designed to come to any hard and fast decisions on specific countries.
"Eurostat will have a news release at noon on Monday on the committee's decisions," she added.

Other EU officials confirmed that such a report would be released and predicted several other evaluations in the coming weeks. But one source said next week's document would not detail decisions on a country-by-country basis.

The question of one-off accounting gimmicks by a number of EU countries has been at the core of a debate over whether they can be considered to have achieved sustainable economic convergence for monetary union.
"It will be issue-by-issue rather than country-by-country," said one EU official.

Among the tax proposals considered will be Italy's "euro-tax" which is designed to raise 5.5 trillion lire. Other contentious areas is the use of gold sales by some countries to lower their outstanding debt ratios.
From Eurostat's evaluation one should be able to infer whether Italy would be allowed to use the tax, which some argue is at odds with EU accounting rules, officials said.
Others noted that the judgements reached may only partially answer some of the outstanding questions financial markets have over 1997 budgets.
Countries wishing to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) will be judged on their economic and budgetary performance in 1997.
Responding to Italy's proposed tax, one official said: "There is indeed a problem and an example of the type of loophole which requires interpretation."
EU officials said Eurostat's verdict on such tax measures would be final.
Should the agency conclude that they are not allowed, then the European Commission, the EU's executive, would adjust its own projections for budgetary performance of the countries affected.
